passages.t: ‘Today the LORD will appear to you’
passages.happening:
“On the eighth day Moses summoned Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel” (verse 1).

He tells Aaron to bring a young bull for a sin offering and a ram for a burnt offering, for himself. The people are to bring a male goat for a sin offering, a calf and a lamb for a burnt offering, an ox and a ram for a peace offering, and a grain offering. “For today the LORD will appear to you” (verse 4).

The whole congregation comes and stands before the LORD. Moses says, “This is what the LORD has commanded you to do, so that the glory of the LORD may appear to you” (verse 6). Then he tells Aaron to go up to the altar.
passages.hearers:
Everything since the end of Exodus has been leading to this day. The tent was built, and God's glory filled it. The offerings were explained. The priests were ordained and waited their seven days. Now comes the question the whole book has been asking. Will it work? Will God in fact meet his people here?

Moses gives the answer in advance, twice: the LORD will appear.

The ‘eighth day’ comes after a finished week of seven. In the Torah an eighth day often marks a new beginning. A boy is circumcised on the eighth day. A person healed of skin disease brings his offerings on the eighth day. Here the priests begin their service.

Aaron's own sin offering is a calf. Later Jewish interpreters saw meaning in that, since the last calf Aaron had dealt with was the golden one.

And all the offerings of chapters 1 to 7 are called for at once: sin offering, burnt offering, grain offering, peace offering. The manual is about to be used for the first time.
passages.later:
The glory Moses promises had been seen before, when the tent was finished: “Then the cloud covered the Tent of Meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). Then it had kept Moses out. Now it will be shown to everyone.

The Hebrew word for glory, kavod, comes from a root that means heavy or weighty. Used of God it often means his presence made visible. John uses the same thought of Jesus: “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us. We have seen His glory” (John 1:14).
passages.asks: The people brought what God asked and then stood and waited for him to appear. Ask what you expect when you come to worship: a duty done, or a meeting with God. And ask when you last waited for him, having done what he asked.

passages.happening:
“So Aaron approached the altar and slaughtered the calf as a sin offering for himself” (verse 8). His sons bring him the blood, and he puts it on the horns of the altar. He burns the fat, and burns the rest outside the camp (verses 9-11). Then he offers his burnt offering, piece by piece (verses 12-14).

“Aaron then presented the people’s offering” (verse 15). He offers their goat for sin, then their burnt offering, then the grain offering, then the ox and the ram as their peace offering (verses 15-18). He burns the fat on the altar and lifts the breasts and the right thigh before the LORD, “as Moses had commanded” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
For the first time Aaron acts as priest. Until now Moses had done everything. Now Aaron goes up to the altar, and his sons hand him the blood and the pieces.

He begins with himself. The priest must be put right with God before he can stand there for anyone else. Every go-between in Israel needed someone to go between for him.

Then he turns to the people, and the order of their offerings has a logic many readers have noticed. First the sin offering, which deals with sin and uncleanness. Then the burnt offering, which gives the whole animal to God. Then the peace offering, the shared meal. Cleansing comes first, then the giving of oneself, then the table.

The passage is plain and careful. It notes that Aaron did things ‘as the LORD had commanded Moses’ (verse 10) and ‘according to the ordinance’ (verse 16). The first day of Israel's worship is done by the book.
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews sums up what Aaron does here: every high priest “is appointed from among men to represent them in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins” (Hebrews 5:1).

When Solomon dedicated the temple centuries later, the same kinds of offering were made, and the same thing followed, as the next passage shows (2 Chronicles 7:1).
passages.asks: Aaron dealt with his own sin before he spoke for anyone else. Ask whether you are quicker to pray about other people's faults than your own. And think about the order: forgiveness, then giving yourself, then the shared table. Ask which of the three you tend to skip.

passages.t: The blessing, the glory and the fire
passages.happening:
“Aaron lifted up his hands toward the people and blessed them” (verse 22). Having made the offerings, he steps down.

“Moses and Aaron then entered the Tent of Meeting. When they came out, they blessed the people, and the glory of the LORD appeared to all the people” (verse 23).

“Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the fat portions on the altar. And when all the people saw it, they shouted for joy and fell facedown” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
This is the high point of the first half of the book. What Moses promised has happened. The glory that filled the tent at the end of Exodus now appears to all the people. And fire from God takes the offering. It is the sign that he accepts it, and that he will live among Israel in the way he has set out.

Lifting the hands toward the people was the gesture of a priest's blessing. A blessing in that world was more than a kind wish. It was a spoken act, said with authority in God's name. The chapter does not give Aaron's words. The book of Numbers later gives the words the priests were to use. In some synagogues, descendants of priestly families still raise their hands to say them.

The people's answer is two things at once. They ‘shouted for joy’: the Hebrew verb is for a ringing cry, the kind heard at festivals. And they ‘fell facedown’, as people did before a king. It is awe and gladness together. Here the fire is a welcome.

The last verse is worded with care. ‘Fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed’ will come again, word for word, two verses later (10:2). This chapter and the next happen on the same day.
passages.later:
The blessing the priests were given to say is in Numbers: “May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:24-26).

When Solomon finished praying at the temple, “fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of the LORD filled the temple” (2 Chronicles 7:1). On Mount Carmel, in Elijah's day, “the fire of the LORD fell and consumed the sacrifice” (1 Kings 18:38).

Luke ends his Gospel with Aaron's gesture. Jesus “lifted up His hands and blessed them” (Luke 24:50). Many readers think Luke means his readers to see a priest's blessing there. It is a link of theme, not a prediction.
passages.asks: The people shouted for joy and fell on their faces in the same moment. Ask whether your sense of God has room for both gladness and awe, or mostly one of them. And receive, slowly, the old words of blessing as spoken to you: the LORD bless you and keep you.
